title: Singapore’s 9.25 GW low-carbon electricity import pipeline outlook
gist: Wood Mackenzie expects low-carbon electricity imports to supply only 15% of Singapore's generation mix by 2035, about half of the one-third EMA target, because none of the 9.25 GW approved capacity has reached financial close; only Malaysia has a credible near-term path.

insights.claim: Singapore approved 9.25 GW of low-carbon import capacity across six corridors, but no project has reached financial close or started construction, and Wood Mackenzie expects imports to be 15% of 2035 generation versus the one-third target.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Decarbonisation targets for Singapore's power sector look likely to be missed, sustaining gas reliance.

insights.claim: Singapore generates up to 95% of electricity from natural gas, and EMA's September 2026 RFP raised planned hydrogen-ready CCGT units for 2032 from two to five.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Gas-fired capacity remains the backbone, supporting gas and turbine demand.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie says challenges are export permits, bankability, cross-border transmission financing and the lack of a market mechanism for Singapore buyers to claim carbon value.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Policy gaps, not technology, hold up delivery.
insights.locator: The most significant challenges for EMA

insights.claim: Indonesia holds 37% of the approved pipeline but is stalled by Clause 37 (five-year renewable export permits revocable if domestic supply is at risk) and a 40% local content requirement, undermining 20-year financing.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Indonesian regulatory risk is the main swing factor for the scheme.

insights.claim: Sovereign wealth fund Danantara was designated in July 2026 to lead cross-border electricity trade with Singapore and signed MOUs with Keppel Electric, Sembcorp Utilities and SGEI, a possible route around the permit problem.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Watch whether Danantara structure extends to electricity exports.
insights.locator: The key development came in July 2026

insights.claim: Malaysia is the only corridor with a credible path this decade: the existing 1 GW HVDC link, 900 MW approved from Johor in August 2026, and Sembcorp's 300 MW could import by 2029.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Malaysia-linked projects are the near-term beneficiaries.

insights.claim: Sarawak's Preferred Supplier Agreement with Prysmian gives it cable-supply certainty others lack, targeting mid-2030s operation.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Subsea cable supply is a bottleneck favoring Prysmian-backed projects.

insights.claim: Vietnam, Cambodia and Australia (43% of the pipeline) have no visible construction timeline; Sun Cable's route has 3,700 km across Indonesian waters and its survey permit does not authorise cable laying.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Sun Cable and similar long-dated projects are high risk.

insights.claim: Imported power must compete with the Uniform Singapore Energy Price of about S$250/MWh and needs an Importer License, 60% annual load factor and offtaker commitment, none of which any project has cleared yet.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Pricing against gas with carbon tax is the final hurdle.
insights.quote: No project in the pipeline has cleared all three hurdles yet.
